Class 1 · Chapter 1 of 8

Tens, ones and number names

Build any number up to 100 from tens and ones.

  1. See it
  2. Try it
  3. Practise it
  4. Print it
  5. Check it

By the end I can…

  • I can build a number with tens and ones.
  • I can match a number to its name.
  • I can compare and order two-digit numbers.

1 See it

Screen 1 of 4

Ten ones make one ten

One small cube is one 'one'.

Ten ones stuck together make a long stick. We call it one 'ten'.

Screen 2 of 4

Read a two-digit number

The number 34 has two digits.

The first digit, 3, tells us the tens. The second digit, 4, tells us the ones.

So 34 is 3 tens and 4 ones.

Screen 3 of 4

Say the number name

Tens have special names: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty.

34 is said 'thirty-four'. Say the tens name, then the ones name.

Screen 4 of 4

Which number is bigger?

Look at the tens first. More tens means a bigger number.

If the tens are the same, look at the ones.

47 is bigger than 38 because 4 tens is more than 3 tens.

Words to know
ones
Single small cubes. Ten ones make one ten.
tens
A stick of ten cubes joined together.
digit
One of the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers.

For parents

What your child learns

Our numbers use place value. In 92, the 9 means 9 tens and the 2 means 2 ones. A ten is a bundle of 10 ones. To compare, look at tens first, then ones.

A common slip

Children often read the digits as separate ones, for example 92 as 9 and 2. Build the number with ten-bundles and single ones. Compare tens first.

5-minute home activity: Tens and ones

  1. Tie or group straws or counters into bundles of 10.
  2. Make 55 with 5 bundles and 5 single ones.
  3. Make 92 and 30 and say which is smaller.
  4. Write the tens and ones on paper beside each number.
